You are helping a researcher prepare for an upcoming academic conference on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). The conference is called "RLHF Summit 2026" and will take place on April 10, 2026 from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM at the San Francisco Convention Center.

First, search the academic paper databases for papers related to "reinforcement learning from human feedback". You should find at least 5 relevant papers. Exclude any papers that are not directly about RLHF or human feedback in the context of language model training (for example, papers about self-play in board games should be excluded).

For each of the relevant RLHF papers you find, retrieve the full manuscript source to examine their methodology sections in detail. Pay attention to the key techniques each paper introduces.

Next, create a PowerPoint presentation called RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx in your workspace. The presentation should include the following slides:

First, a title slide with the title "RLHF Summit 2026 Conference Preparation Report" and subtitle "Key Papers in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback".

First, an overview slide that introduces the field of RLHF and why it matters for language model alignment.

First, one slide for each of the relevant papers (at least 5 slides). Each paper slide should include the paper title, the authors, and a brief summary of the key contribution and methodology. Make sure to include papers about instruction following with human feedback, learning to summarize from human feedback, constitutional AI, direct preference optimization, and proximal policy optimization.

First, a summary slide that synthesizes the key themes across all papers.

After creating the presentation, create a calendar event for the RLHF Summit 2026 conference. The event should be on April 10, 2026 from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, with the location set to "San Francisco Convention Center" and a description that mentions this is a conference about reinforcement learning from human feedback.

Finally, send an email to your collaborators at collaborators@rlhf-lab.org with the subject "RLHF Summit 2026 Preparation Materials". The email body should briefly describe that you have prepared a conference report covering key RLHF papers and created a calendar event for the conference. Mention the date (April 10, 2026) and location in the email.

If you are working in a multi-agent setup, designate exactly one agent to create and write RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx, and have the other agents coordinate with it — do not have multiple agents write to the same file, as concurrent writers can overwrite each other.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:

Before Wave 1, the main agent must freeze exactly five required paper slots—InstructGPT, learning to summarize from human feedback, Constitutional AI, DPO, and PPO—and the conference, presentation, calendar, and email contract. I am preparing for an academic conference on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) called "RLHF Summit 2026". I need you to search academic paper databases for relevant papers.

Use the `mcp__scholarly__search-arxiv` and `mcp__scholarly__search-google-scholar` tools with the keyword "reinforcement learning from human feedback" (and related queries like "RLHF", "human feedback language model alignment", "direct preference optimization", "constitutional AI").

Your task:
1. Run several searches with the keyword "reinforcement learning from human feedback" and related terms.
2. Identify at least 5 relevant papers. The papers MUST be directly about RLHF or human feedback in the context of language model training. Specifically, I need papers covering these topics (each likely corresponds to one paper):
   - Instruction following with human feedback (InstructGPT)
   - Learning to summarize from human feedback
   - Constitutional AI (harmlessness from AI feedback)
   - Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)
   - Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) - note: PPO is the foundational RL algorithm used in RLHF
3. EXCLUDE any papers that are NOT directly about RLHF or human feedback for language models (e.g., papers about self-play in board games like AlphaZero, or generic robotics RL papers without human feedback).

For each relevant paper you find, report back:
- The exact paper title
- The arXiv ID (e.g., "2203.02155") — this is critical, as I will use it to fetch the full source
- The full author list
- A 1-2 sentence description of what the paper is about
- Confirmation it is directly relevant to RLHF for language models

Report back a list of at least 5 confirmed-relevant papers with their arXiv IDs. Also list any papers you found that you excluded and why (briefly). Do not create, modify, or write any files — just report your findings.

# Task
Create a PowerPoint presentation at this exact path:
`/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_GLM-5.3/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-conference-prep/workspace/RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx`

Filename must be exactly `RLHF_Conference_Report.pptx`.

# Context
I am preparing for an academic conference, "RLHF Summit 2026" (April 10, 2026, 9:00 AM–5:00 PM, San Francisco Convention Center), on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). I searched scholarly databases, retrieved the full manuscript sources of 5 relevant RLHF papers, and analyzed their methodologies. The deck must present these findings. You are building the deliverable from the research content below — do not go out and search for more papers.

# Required structure — exactly 8 slides, in this order

## Slide 1 — Title slide
- Title: `RLHF Summit 2026 Conference Preparation Report`
- Subtitle: `Key Papers in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback`

## Slide 2 — Overview: "RLHF: Overview and Why It Matters"
Introduce the field of RLHF and why it matters for language model alignment. Cover:
- What RLHF is: a post-training alignment technique that optimizes a language model against a learned model of human preferences rather than only a next-token prediction objective.
- The canonical three-stage recipe: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on human demonstrations; (2) train a reward model on human preference comparisons; (3) optimize the policy against that reward model with reinforcement learning, regularized by a KL penalty to stay close to the reference model.
- Why it matters: pretraining objectives capture likelihood, not helpfulness, truthfulness or harmlessness — RLHF closes the gap between next-token prediction and human intent.
- Impact evidence: an aligned 1.3B-parameter model (InstructGPT) is preferred by human evaluators over an unaligned 175B-parameter model — alignment can matter more than scale.
- RLHF underpins modern instruction-following assistants and launched an active research agenda: scalable feedback (RLAIF), simpler offline objectives (DPO), and stable optimization (PPO).

## Slides 3–7 — One slide per paper
Each of these 5 slides must include the paper title, the authors, the arXiv ID/year, and a concise summary of the key contribution and methodology. Suggested layout: title = short paper handle; body = "Authors:" line, then "Key contribution:" and "Methodology:" bullet groups.

### Slide 3 — InstructGPT
- Title: `Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback (InstructGPT)`
- arXiv 2203.02155 · 2022 (NeurIPS)
- Authors: Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, Diogo Almeida, Carroll Wainwright, Pamela Mishkin, Chong Zhang, Sandhini Agarwal, Katarina Slama, Alex Ray, John Schulman
- Key contribution: Aligns GPT-3 with user intent using human feedback instead of scale; the resulting 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT is preferred by human evaluators over the 175B-parameter GPT-3, while being more truthful and less toxic.
- Methodology: A three-stage RLHF pipeline — (1) supervised fine-tuning on labeler demonstrations; (2) a reward model trained on human labeler rankings of model outputs; (3) PPO optimization of the policy against the reward model, with a KL penalty keeping the policy close to the original model. Evaluated via human preference head-to-head comparisons, TruthfulQA (truthfulness) and RealToxicityPrompts (toxicity).

### Slide 4 — Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback
- Title: `Learning to Summarize from Human Feedback`
- arXiv 2009.01325 · 2020 (NeurIPS)
- Authors: Nisan Stiennon, Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Daniel Ziegler, Ryan Lowe, Chelsea Voss, Alec Radford, Dario Amodei, Paul Christiano
- Key contribution: Foundational demonstration of the "reward model + RL fine-tuning" paradigm, applied to abstractive summarization of Reddit posts — RLHF-trained summaries beat supervised learning baselines on human preference.
- Methodology: A reward model is trained from human comparisons of summaries, taking a (post, summary) pair and outputting a scalar reward. That reward model replaces a proxy metric and is used as the reward function to fine-tune the supervised summarization policy with PPO. A KL penalty against the supervised baseline prevents reward-model over-optimization and preserves language quality. On the Reddit TL;DR dataset, human evaluators preferred the RL-trained summaries 61% of the time over the supervised baseline.

### Slide 5 — Constitutional AI
- Title: `Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback`
- arXiv 2212.08073 · 2022
- Authors: Yuntao Bai, Saurav Kadavath, Sandipan Kundu, Amanda Askell, Jackson Kernion, Andy Jones, Anna Chen, Anna Goldie, Azalia Mirhoseini, Cameron McKinnon, et al. (40 authors, Anthropic)
- Key contribution: Introduces Constitutional AI (CAI), training a harmless AI assistant using AI feedback (RLAIF) guided by an explicit, human-written set of principles — a "constitution" — instead of human harmlessness labels.
- Methodology: Two phases. (1) Critique–revision supervised stage: the model critiques its own responses to red-team prompts against constitutional principles and produces revisions; fine-tuning on these self-generated revisions creates a harmlessness dataset with no human harmlessness labels. (2) RL stage: a preference model is trained on AI-generated preference comparisons conditioned on the constitution, and that preference model provides the reward signal for RL fine-tuning. The constitution spans helpfulness, harmlessness and honesty; resulting models are both more helpful and more harmless than RLHF-trained ones while greatly reducing the need for human red-teaming labels.

### Slide 6 — Direct Preference Optimization
- Title: `Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model (DPO)`
- arXiv 2305.18290 · 2023 (NeurIPS)
- Authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn
- Key contribution: Optimizes the same objective as RLHF pipelines — maximum reward under a KL-divergence constraint relative to a reference policy — using only preference data, without explicitly fitting a reward model, sampling from the LM during training, or extensive hyperparameter tuning.
- Methodology: Exploits a mapping between reward functions and optimal policies: because the optimal policy under KL-constrained reward maximization has a closed form in terms of the reward, the reward model can be eliminated and the policy optimized directly over preferred/dispreferred pairs with a simple binary cross-entropy classification loss — turning RL into supervised learning. Evaluated on summarization and dialogue; matches or exceeds PPO-based RLHF, with win rates on TL;DR similar to PPO while requiring fewer hyperparameters.

### Slide 7 — Proximal Policy Optimization
- Title: `Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms (PPO)`
- arXiv 1707.06347 · 2017
- Authors: John Schulman, Filip Wolski, Prafulla Dhariwal, Alec Radford, Oleg Klimov
- Key contribution: Introduces a family of policy gradient methods that alternate between sampling data via interaction and optimizing a clipped surrogate objective, enabling multiple epochs of minibatch updates per batch of data — retaining TRPO's stability while being far simpler and more general. PPO became the foundation algorithm used in RLHF pipelines.
- Methodology: The clipped surrogate objective L^CLIP = E[min(r_t A_t, clip(r_t, 1-eps, 1+eps) A_t)], where r_t is the probability ratio between the new and old policy and A_t is the advantage estimate; clipping the ratio to [1-eps, 1+eps] prevents destructively large policy updates, removing TRPO's constrained-optimization machinery. The full loss combines the clipped policy surrogate, a value-function (critic) loss, and an entropy bonus for exploration. Originally evaluated on Atari and MuJoCo; in RLHF it is applied to the policy against the reward model with a KL penalty to the reference policy.

## Slide 8 — Summary: "Key Themes Across the Papers"
Synthesize the key themes across all five papers:
- A shared recipe: learn a reward signal from preference comparisons, then optimize the policy against it with KL-regularized reinforcement learning.
- Alignment beats scale: a 1.3B aligned model (InstructGPT) is preferred over a 175B unaligned one.
- Stability is the crux: PPO's clipped surrogate objective plus the KL penalty to the reference policy are the two mechanisms that keep RLHF training stable and prevent reward-model over-optimization.
- From RL to classification: DPO re-parameterizes the same KL-constrained objective as a supervised loss over preference pairs, removing the reward model and online sampling.
- Scaling the feedback: Stiennon et al. and InstructGPT depend on human labelers; Constitutional AI replaces them with principle-guided AI feedback (RLAIF), pointing toward scalable oversight.
- Evaluation shifted from automatic metrics to human preference evaluation — win rates, TruthfulQA, RealToxicityPrompts.
- Timeline of the field: PPO (2017) → RLHF for summarization (2020) → instruction following at scale (2022) → RLAIF (2022) → offline preference optimization with DPO (2023).

# Quality requirements
- Every slide must be readable: no text overflowing or spilling outside the slide or placeholders. Keep bullets tight; trim wording rather than shrinking text below ~12pt. For long author lists you may write "First Author, Second Author, Third Author, et al." — but Slide 4 (Stiennon et al.) and Slide 6 (Rafailov et al.) must list ALL authors in full.
- Use a consistent, professional look (a modern/corporate color scheme is fine).
- Do not add extra slides beyond the 8 described. Do not skip any.

# Acceptance criteria / verification before you report back
1. The file exists at the exact path above.
2. Extract the presentation text and confirm: 8 slides total; slide 1 has the exact title "RLHF Summit 2026 Conference Preparation Report" and subtitle "Key Papers in Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback"; slides 3–7 each contain a distinct paper title plus an authors section; slide 8 synthesizes themes.
3. Report back the final slide count, the file path, and the extracted title of each slide so I can verify.

Do not create the calendar event or send any email — I am handling those separately. Do not write any other files besides this presentation.
